title: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting (part 2 of 3)
sources: Positions: authored, replayed with python-chess, engine-checked by tools/validate_lessons.py

steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting. This part covers Hidden helpers and false defenders; Stop in time. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: Two rooks doubled on the d-file. Only the front rook attacks the knight directly; the rear one waits behind it.

line.say: The front rook takes the knight: +3.
Black's rook takes back: -5. Total -2 for now.
The rear rook, which was hidden behind the first, takes again: +5. Total +3.

steps.caption: Take away the rear rook and nothing is left to take back. A lone rook against a defended knight loses.

line.say: Black's rook takes back: -5. White is 2 points down and has no helper.

steps.text: A piece behind another on the same file, rank or diagonal can join in once the front one has gone, but only if it moves along that line: two rooks on a file, a queen behind a bishop on a diagonal. A rook behind a bishop on a diagonal does not. Count such pieces, and the same goes for the defending side.

steps.caption: Not a battery. The rook on a2 stands behind the bishop on the same diagonal, but a rook cannot move along a diagonal, so it never joins the fight on d5.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop: -3. The rook behind could not take part.

steps.text: A defender only counts if it can really capture. A piece that is **pinned**, meaning it may not move because that would leave its own king in check, cannot take back. Edward Lasker warned in *Chess Strategy* that a defender can be an illusion for reasons like this. So after counting, ask about every defender: could it legally capture right now? A pin to the king makes a recapture illegal; a pin to a bigger piece only makes it costly.

steps.caption: The pawn on d7 looks like a defender of the knight. But the bishop on b5 pins it against the king.

line.say: The rook takes the knight with check. The d7 pawn cannot take back: moving would leave its king in check.
The king steps aside (Kf8 or Kd8). White has won a whole knight.

steps.text: The king can capture too, but never onto a square a defender guards. So a king is usually the last attacker or the last defender, and it counts only when nothing is left to take it back. Count it last.

steps.caption: The king touches the rook on d2, but the knight on b3 defends it. The king cannot take.

steps.text: You do not have to finish the swaps. After each capture, look at what is left and ask whether the next capture would give up more than it gains. If so, stop there. Counting well means knowing how many captures to make, not only how many are possible. Next: two attackers against two defenders, and White still comes out ahead.

steps.caption: Two attackers (pawn and rook), two defenders (pawn and rook). The target is a knight, and the pawn is the cheapest piece here.

line.say: Black's pawn takes back: -1. White is 2 points up, and this is the place to stop.

steps.caption: Why stop? The pawn on d5 is attacked once and defended once, and White's attacker is a rook.

line.say: Black's rook takes back: -5. White would be 4 points down on this swap.
